clinicalPearls: Rare, severe multisystem telomere biology disorder at the severe end of the dyskeratosis congenita spectrum, overlapping clinically with Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson syndrome.
Most cases are caused by heterozygous, frequently de novo, TINF2 variants affecting the shelterin protein TIN2, producing extremely short telomeres.
The hallmark is bilateral exudative (Coats-like) retinopathy with retinal vascular abnormalities, exudates and a high risk of detachment, presenting in infancy or early childhood.
Bone marrow failure and aplastic anaemia typically develop in early childhood and are a major cause of death.
Neurological features include intracranial calcification, cerebellar hypoplasia and psychomotor impairment.
Intrauterine growth restriction, fine sparse hair and nail changes are often present.
Diagnosis rests on very short leucocyte telomeres (flow-FISH) with TINF2 sequencing.
reference.pathophysiology: Revesz syndrome sits within the telomere biology disorder spectrum and is caused chiefly by pathogenic variants in TINF2, which encodes TIN2, a core component of the six-protein shelterin complex that caps and protects telomeres and links the double-stranded telomeric binding proteins TRF1 and TRF2 to the TPP1-POT1 module. Disease-associated TINF2 variants, which cluster in a mutational hotspot, destabilise telomere protection and impair telomerase recruitment, producing extremely short telomeres and premature replicative senescence or apoptosis in proliferative tissues. The severity of telomere shortening explains the early, multisystem phenotype: failure of the haematopoietic compartment (aplastic anaemia), a distinctive bilateral exudative (Coats-type) retinopathy arising from retinal microvascular compromise, and central nervous system involvement with cerebellar hypoplasia and intracranial calcification, features that overlap with Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson syndrome (severe infantile dyskeratosis congenita) — overlapping and often allelic
Coats disease (usually isolated and unilateral exudative retinopathy)
Coats plus syndrome / CRMCC (CTC1-related, with intracranial calcification and cysts)
Retinoblastoma (in the differential diagnosis of leucocoria)
Other inherited bone marrow failure syndromes such as Fanconi anaemia
Congenital (TORCH) infections presenting with retinopathy and intracranial calcification
additionalInvestigations: TINF2 sequencing, with a broader telomere-gene panel if negative
Full blood count and bone marrow examination with cytogenetics
Dilated fundoscopy and retinal imaging, with examination under anaesthesia in young children
Neuroimaging (MRI/CT) for cerebellar hypoplasia and intracranial calcification
Chromosome breakage study to exclude Fanconi anaemia
redFlags: Leucocoria or exudative retinal detachment threatening vision
Progressive pancytopenia or marrow failure requiring transfusion or transplant assessment
Failure to thrive with developmental regression
reference.prognosis: Poor; the combination of early aplastic anaemia, progressive retinopathy and neurological involvement usually leads to death in childhood, although the course varies with severity.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the retinopathy as isolated Coats disease and missing the systemic telomere disorder
Attributing retinopathy together with intracranial calcification solely to congenital infection
Using standard-intensity transplant conditioning, which is poorly tolerated in telomere biology disorders
Assuming autosomal recessive inheritance when many TINF2 cases are de novo dominant
references: Dyskeratosis congenita and telomere biology disorder reviews
Inherited bone marrow failure syndrome guidelines
